items.title: In 1994, Oasis was sued for $500,000 by Coca-Cola for a song that sounded very similar to an iconic ad
items.summary:
As the adage goes, “All musicians are thieves,” and no one has lived up to the title quite like Britpop kings, Oasis. The great thing is that they are completely unapologetic about their love of paying tribute to other artists by lifting their melodies, riffs, and lyrics.

The piano intro to “Don’t Look Back in Anger” sounds like John Lennon’s “Imagine.” The main riff to “Cigarettes and Alcohol” is “Bang a Gong” by T. Rex. The song “Step Out” sounded so much like “Uptight (Everything Is Alright)” by Steve Wonder that they took it off an album and made it a B-side. They still got sued by Wonder and his co-writers. The list goes on and on.

It’s one thing to get sued by fellow musicians for repurposing their ideas, but in 1994, just after the release of their debut album Definitely Maybe , Oasis was sued by a major multinational corporation, Coca-Cola, for their second single “Shakermaker.” Not bad for 5 kids who grew up in working-class Manchester, England. 

Coca-Cola claimed that the band ripped off “I’d Like to Teach the World to Sing (In Perfect Harmony),” a song it used in an iconic 1971 ad campaign, and they most certainly did. In fact, in early concerts, the band sang lyrics to the song in the opening:

I’d like to teach the world to sing 

In perfect harmony 

I’d like to buy the world a Coke 

And keep it company 

The band changed the lyrics to:

I’d like to be somebody else 

And not know where I’ve been 

I’d like to build myself a house 

Out of plasticine 

The Coca-Cola ad was so popular that The New Seekers re-recorded the song and released it as a single…
items.t: In 1994, Oasis was sued for $500,000 by Coca-Cola for a song that sounded very similar to an iconic ad

items.title: Fred Astaire made a hat rack look like a dance partner. Watch the moment he lets go.
items.summary:
Most people probably know Fred Astaire for his flawless dances with stars like Ginger Rogers and Rita Hayworth. But even more impressive, some of his most iconic routines involved a dance partner who wasn’t human at all. 

Case in point: his hat rack routine from Royal Wedding .

In the 1951 musical, Astaire’s character, Tom Bowen, is rehearsing while his dance partner and sister, Ellen, is absent. Sans a human partner, Astaire dances to “Sunday Jumps” using whatever happens to be around him, including an unassuming hat rack. 

In true Astaire form, he made this unlikely pairing come to life in the most magical way. 

Astaire doesn’t just dance with the hat rack 

It’s really not just that Astaire adeptly and gracefully moves around the room with this piece of furniture. It was his remarkable ability to commit to the idea that this rack was another performer.

This gift was even noted in a recent academic study of the MGM musical , which commended Astaire for transforming the “inanimate object into a whirling ‘dervish’ of excitement that pirouettes on his every command because he gave it the same attention and focus he would give a “human dance partner.”

Another way of putting it: Astaire wasn’t necessarily trying to convince the audience that the hat rack was a person. But he was, in his own way, offering the object the same level of respect that we would a person. In the routine, at least. 

Watch the moment he lets go 

To this point, there’s one particularly cool moment when Astaire gets the rack moving and releases it. For a beat, it keeps going without him.

That…
items.t: Fred Astaire made a hat rack look like a dance partner. Watch the moment he lets go.

items.title: A 79-year-old went to beauty school to help his wife of 50 years. Her eyesight was failing.
items.summary:
One quiet afternoon in April 2021, a man in his late 70s knocked on the door of Delmar College of Hair & Esthetics in Red Deer, Alberta, and asked whether they offered courses.

“I said that we sure do,” director Carrie Hannah told Red Deer News Now . Then he explained why he was asking. His wife’s vision was going , and she kept burning herself with her curling iron .

“He said, ‘I’d really like to be able to help her but I don’t know how,’” Hannah recalled.

View this post on Instagram 

His wife of 50 years had always taken pride in her appearance, Hannah said, “and it’s important to her, so therefore important to him.”

The school paired him with a student, Britney Smith, and a mannequin head. Over about an hour, she taught him to set volume curls on short hair and how to keep the hot iron away from his wife’s skin. Then he had one more request: his wife had been poking herself in the eye with her mascara wand.

“He also asked for tips on applying mascara because that task was hard for her also, so we gave him a makeup lesson too!” Hannah told SWNS, according to People .

Throughout the lesson, he kept pulling photos of his wife out of his wallet to show the room, from every age. “Bragging on what a beautiful and wonderful wife she is,” Hannah said. She’d been a courtroom stenographer who could type more than 100 words a minute. He even got a haircut himself before he left.

Smith ( @hairdesignbybritney on Instagram) posted photos of the lesson on-line and they reached hundreds of thousands by the next morning. The man, who asked to stay anonymous, was turning 80 that…
items.t: A 79-year-old went to beauty school to help his wife of 50 years. Her eyesight was failing.

items.title: 1,000 Swiss volunteers buried their underwear for science. It just won an Ig Nobel Prize.
items.summary:
In 2021, about 1,000 people across Switzerland got an unusual package in the mail: two pairs of brand-new white cotton underwear , along with instructions to bury them.

It was a citizen science project called “ Proof by Underpants ,” run by the University of Zurich and Agroscope , Switzerland’s federal agricultural research center. The idea was simple. Bacteria, fungi, earthworms and other soil organisms eat cotton and the more life there is in a patch of ground, the faster a pair of underwear disappears.

View this post on Instagram 

Volunteers buried more than 2,000 pairs, along with 12,000 tea bags, at roughly 1,000 sites around the country: private gardens, lawns, meadows and farm fields. Two months later, they dug them back up, photographed what was left and mailed the remains to the lab with soil samples.

“People don’t realize that 50 percent of all living species live in the soil,” said Marcel van der Heijden, a University of Zurich professor who co-led the study.

View this post on Instagram 

The results, published in August in the journal Plants, People, Planet , showed huge differences. Underwear buried in private gardens decomposed fastest, thanks to soil rich in organic matter and teeming with life. Underwear in lawns held up the best. Farm fields and meadows fell in between, and organic fields broke the cotton down faster than conventional ones. The biggest predictor wasn’t the soil’s chemistry, but what people did with the land.

“Our results show that how soil is managed can significantly affect both soil life and soil quality,” van der Heijden said in a…
items.t: 1,000 Swiss volunteers buried their underwear for science. It just won an Ig Nobel Prize.

items.title: Neuroscience expert explains 5 ways to become ‘unrecognizable’ 6 months from now
items.summary:
For some, the idea of changing things we don’t like about ourselves seems insurmountable. Perhaps this is because we think we need to make giant, bold leaps for reinvention. In reality, we don’t actually need huge moves to make changes. A neuroscience expert explains there are tiny daily actions we can take in order to slowly but surely change who we are.

In a clip posted to Instagram, neuroscience expert Tina Levinson ( @rewiredmanifor online) discusses ways in which we can slowly change whatever version of ourselves we’d like to improve. As she sits in a pink sweater with two small dogs biting on sticks in her lap, a chyron appears which reads: “If I wanted to become an unrecognizable version of myself six months from now, these are the five things I’d practice every day.”

Tina, Neuroscience Coach, Instagram 

She adds, “I say this as a neuroscience coach who had to use these exact practices to rebuild my own life. And none of them are big. Because this is what I think we get completely wrong about becoming a different person. We focus on the giant transformation, when your brain is actually changing in these tiny, almost boring moments throughout the day.”

Question just one thought 

First she suggests to “question just one thought.” She explains, “Because your brain hands you predictions all day long disguised as facts, right? ‘I can’t do this. This is gonna go badly. They’re gonna judge me.’ And instead of immediately believing it, I’d ask, ‘Do I actually know that?’ That one question creates a tiny gap between what your brain predicts and what you choose to do.”…
items.t: Neuroscience expert explains 5 ways to become ‘unrecognizable’ 6 months from now

items.title: America once had a federal official whose job included answering ‘What shall we have for dinner?’
items.summary:
During the 1920s , radios had a boom in the United States. Sales of radios went from $60 million in 1922 to $426 million in 1929, according to the University of Houston Digital History . 

Families began to gather around their radios and listen to comedies, musical variety shows and news. And the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Bureau of Home Economics and Farm Radio Service decided to create its own 15-minute broadcast aimed at housewives and all things homemaking in a number of different segments.

The show, called Housekeeper Chat , centered on the fictional character Aunt Sammy, the wife of Uncle Sam (the famous United State’s federal government persona). It premiered on October 4, 1926.

Aunt Sammy’s radio segments, explained 

The 15-minute Housekeeper Chat show was broken down into three, 5-minute segments: “Backyard Gossip”, “Questions Women are Asking”, and “What Shall We Have For Dinner?”. 

Real women took on the role of Aunt Sammy, including: Ruth Van DeMan , a home economics specialist who created many of Aunt Sammy’s recipes and menus; Josephine Hemphill , a journalism teacher who graduated from of Kansas State Agricultural College, who wrote many of the conversational scripts; and Fanny Walker Yeatman, who both tested and tasted recipes that were created for the show by the Bureau of Home Economics. 

Final show approvals were run through another woman, Dr. Louise Stanley, head of the Bureau of Home Economics, before the show aired.

Ruth Van DeMan told a newspaper in 1927, “This is no caviar and truffle service for jazz-jaded appetites. We are striving to…
items.t: America once had a federal official whose job included answering ‘What shall we have for dinner?’

items.title: Before Natalie Imbruglia sang ‘Torn,’ its songwriter recorded a version with a very different bite
items.summary:
No soundtrack of the 1990s would be complete without Natalie Imbruglia’s “Torn.” The hit single was one of the biggest songs of the 90s, topping the radio charts for 11 weeks. It’s widely recognized as one of the most popular and influential pop songs ever.

The hook was catchy, Imbruglia’s Australian voice was unique and infectious, and the lyrics were relatable to anyone who’d ever been disillusioned or felt alone even inside of a romantic relationship.

The song was so popular, in fact, that it charted all over the world. “Torn” was a hit in Canada, Belgium, Denmark, Spain, and more. Truly iconic.

Imbruglia’s “Torn” was, surprisingly, a cover 

What many people don’t realize about the song that immediately evokes all things 90s is that Imbruglia was not the original songwriter or even performer of “Torn.”

“Torn” was written by Anne Preven along with Scott Cutler and Phil Thornalley in 1991, a full six years before Imbruglia’s version was released. Preven and Cutler were members of the California rock band Ednaswap.

Ednaswap’s version of “Torn” was wildly different from the version many of us have grown to love. Instead of the lighthearted, whimsical music backing the lyrics and a synthetic beat, Ednaswap performed the song with guitars and heavy drums.

Preven’s voice brought a completely different flavor to the lyrics, as well, as she infused it with far more grit; giving the song a mood of anger and frustration, along with a little bit of an edge.

Even Ednaswap was not the first to record “Torn” 

Preven and her bandmates, along with Phil Thornalley, wrote “Torn”…
items.t: Before Natalie Imbruglia sang ‘Torn,’ its songwriter recorded a version with a very different bite

items.title: People are ‘Frankensteining’ their partners. Therapists explain what that actually means.
items.summary:
Dr. Frankenstein learned the hard way that he couldn’t piece together a human to his own liking. But centuries later, it seems that people haven’t quite figured that out. 

“Frankensteining” is a buzzy term for attempting to mold your significant other into your idea of a perfect partner, rather than embracing their own unique personality. 

While this version might not be quite as messy as what’s depicted in the Mary Shelley novel, experts agree it doesn’t exactly lead to a healthy relationship. 

Upworthy spoke with several relationship experts about what “Frankensteining” looks like, why people do it, and how to tell when a desire for change has crossed a line. Here’s what they had to say. 

What “Frankensteining” looks like 

As Dr. Karen Stewart, Psy.D. notes, this behavior is “nothing new.” Unrealistic relationship expectations, perfectionism, or a need for control in a relationship can cause someone to fall in love with their partner’s potential rather than who they actually are. 

“Frankensteining often starts subtly and can even be disguised as love or concern,” she warns, “such as encouraging your partner to dress differently, lose weight, change their social circle, become more ambitious, or adopt your interests.”

She adds that “individually, these suggestions may seem harmless, but over time, they can create a dynamic where one partner feels they are constantly being evaluated or corrected.”

What “Frankensteining” is not 

Frankensteining is different from asking that a partner change a specific behavior (example: “Can you text me if you’ll be late?”), which…
items.t: People are ‘Frankensteining’ their partners. Therapists explain what that actually means.

items.title: Ella Fitzgerald forgot the words to ‘Mack the Knife.’ Her improvised version earned a Grammy.
items.summary:
Standing on stage in front of a crowd is already terrifying for many people. But being in the spotlight, with all eyes on you, and making a big mistake? Total nightmare fuel. 

Unless you’re Ella Fitzgerald, who turned an on-stage oopsies into an award-winning triumph.

The iconic jazz singer took the stage in Berlin, Germany , on February 13, 1960, to sing “Mack the Knife.” But partway through the song, she completely blanked on the lyrics. 

She didn’t miss a beat 

Did Ella panic? Nope. She just kept right on singing the tune with the first words that came to her head:

Oh, what’s the next chorus to this song now?
This is the one now, I don’t know
But it was a swingin’ tune and it’s a hit soon
So we tried to do Mack the Knife 

She kept going in this improvised fashion for nearly two minutes, conjuring lyrics out of thin air. The most impressive part was that the words not only matched the tune and rhythm of the song, but many of them even fit the rhyme scheme. 

She even joked about her own flub-up within the impromptu lyrics, referencing Bobby Darin and Louis Armstrong, who originally made the song popular:

Oh, Bobby Darin and Louis Armstrong
They made a record, oh, but they did
And now Ella, Ella and her fellas
We’re makin’ a wreck, what a wreck of Mack the Knife 

That live flub-up won her a Grammy 

Ella Fitzgerald was a global sensation at this point in her career, so maybe audiences would have forgiven the hiccup even if she’d stopped and restarted the song. But the fact that she didn’t skip a beat simply solidified her status as a musical icon. 

Of course, it…
items.t: Ella Fitzgerald forgot the words to ‘Mack the Knife.’ Her improvised version earned a Grammy.

items.title: An art teacher left after 20 years to drive trucks. Her audio diary explains why.
items.summary:
Joan Cross spent 20 years as a passionate art teacher for K-8 grades in the Lakes Region of New Hampshire. But after a noticeable slide in student behavior and other teaching challenges, she decided to make a major career move: to become a commercial truck driver .

Cross had been documenting her feelings about changing dynamics in her career and with her students in a personal audio diary. 

“It was helpful to make those recordings instead of writing things down,” shared in a 2023 interview with New Hampshire Public Radio .

Cross offered more details on her audio diary and her decision to leave education for truck driving.

“I’m not a school counselor. I’m not a psychologist,” she told NHPR’s Morning Edition host Rick Ganley. “And it felt like those were skills that I needed in order to get through my school day instead of just teaching art.”

Cross’s career as an art teacher in changing times 

In one profound audio diary entry, Cross said:

“I’ve spent thousands of dollars and thousands of hours to be an educator. I have a master’s degree. I’ve been doing this for 20 years, and I don’t recognize my profession anymore. Just the social-emotional skill level of these students is unrecognizable. “

Cross added that her classroom and the focus on making art was “falling apart”, noting that following the COVID-19 pandemic, behavioral issues were magnified.

“[They were] having emotional issues. I’d have kids wailing, or I’d have kids that are growling at me, literally growling,” Cross added. “They will wreck a room, they’ll just flip a table. And I’m not equipped to help…
items.t: An art teacher left after 20 years to drive trucks. Her audio diary explains why.

items.title: The City That Kicked Out Cars Before It Was Cool
items.summary:
A s a taxi driver, Juan Barbosa should in theory be one of the strongest opponents of a crackdown on cars. But, puffing on a cigarette beside his vehicle on a sultry August afternoon, the inhabitant of Pontevedra, Spain, admits that he finds himself in something of an existential crisis. 

“As a driver, I suffer,” says Barbosa, who has been ferrying passengers around the northwestern city for two decades. “We can’t enter certain areas unless we have a customer or a booking. We have to take longer routes. But as a pedestrian, life is better. I enjoy it when there are fewer vehicles around.” 

Post-pandemic, pedestrian-first urban planning is now all the rage, from 15-minute cities to low-traffic zones and the rise of soft mobility ( human-powered or low-emission electric transport). But Pontevedra, which is home to 85,000 people in the city and just under a million in the province, was way ahead of the curve. It technically began its war on cars last century. (In 1999, to be precise.) 

The urban transformation of Pontevedra was carried out gradually, over the course of several years. Credit: Peter Yeung 
 Today Pontevedra, which fittingly is located on one of the world-famous Camino de Santiago pilgrimage routes , is considered perhaps the greatest example in the world when it comes to getting rid of cars. Every year, delegations of mayors, professors and city planners make their own pilgrimage to learn about this great vanishing act. 

“Pontevedra is an influential example and something we speak of often,” says Mark Nieuwenhuijsen , director of the urban planning,…
items.t: The City That Kicked Out Cars Before It Was Cool

items.title: Montreal Is Harnessing Soothing Ocean Sounds to Combat Traffic Noise
items.summary:
P arc des Madelinots, a humble wedge of green space in the Verdun borough of Montreal, is not in the most tranquil of settings. The 6,500-square-foot pocket park sits beside a busy junction and is flanked on two sides by roads often filled with cars. 

For years, locals in the historically working-class neighborhood had to deal with the noise of constant passing vehicle traffic while trying to relax, meet with friends, play with their kids or, indeed, do anything else in this outdoor community space.  

But today, Parc des Madelinots is bathed in a very different kind of sound: the lap of ocean waves, dulcet bird calls and the crunch of sand underfoot. 

Reasons to Be Cheerful · Parc des Madelinots Soundscape 
 It’s not because a beach has suddenly arrived in Verdun. The sounds are recordings being broadcast in an attempt to reshape urban noise, fighting sound with sound in a constructive way to reduce noise-induced disturbance, reinvigorate the use of the public space and even preserve cultural memory for displaced communities. 

“Sound is more than just noise, it can be a powerful resource,” says Catherine Guastavino, a professor at McGill University and principal investigator of Sounds in the City , a research team that is one of the collaborators on Les Madelinéennes , the sonic project in Parc des Madelinots. “We can use sounds to improve people’s experience of places.”
